question.text: Chapter 9 describes MBO (Management Buyout) as a common form of LBO. In the example given, ABC is a listed entity where management holds 25% and the public holds 75%. For a valid MBO, management must end up holding:

answer.text: At least 51% (controlling interest) — by purchasing enough shares from the public.
At least 10% to keep operational skin-in-the-game.
Exactly 100% — all public shareholders must be squeezed out.
At least 75% — equivalent to SEBI takeover delisting threshold.

explanation.text: **The Logic:** Chapter 9 example: 'the current management will purchase enough shares from the public so that it can end up holding at least 51 per cent of the stock.' The defining characteristic of an MBO (and LBO generally) is the 51% control threshold, not 100% buyout. **The Trap:** Option B is way below control. Option C is an extreme squeeze-out — not the Chapter 9 example. Option D confuses MBO with delisting threshold (90% per SEBI Delisting Regulations). **Cross-Exam Context:** XV tests MBO economics in CA/CFA-style equity analysis. XIX-A covers MBO concept at distributor level. III-A/C (Compliance) covers takeover disclosure thresholds. **Manager's Pro-Tip:** In an MBO, design a post-close management equity plan (typically 8-12% reserved for managers via ESOPs or phantom units). This aligns management with LP returns and is a standard GP discipline. The PPM should disclose ESOP dilution upfront.
